intents.name: live_disruption_status
intents.definition: Customer asks for real‑time information about a specific train’s delay, cancellation, driver absence or platform, or wants to know if a service is running now.
intents.hard_case: “The 08:02 from Maidenhead is always late, why?” – This is a punctuality explanation (historical pattern) not a live status request, so it belongs to punctuality_explanation.
intents.disposition_rationale: Answers require up‑to‑date running data that the bot cannot guarantee; a human should verify before replying.

intents.name: punctuality_explanation
intents.definition: Customer seeks an explanation for recurring lateness or systematic delay of a service, not a current status.
intents.hard_case: “Hi, what time will the delayed 07:53 TWY‑PAD get to PAD?” – This asks for the current expected arrival, so it belongs to live_disruption_status.
intents.disposition_rationale: A standard template explaining typical causes of lateness can be safely sent.

intents.name: ticket_purchase_and_booking
intents.definition: Customer needs help buying, printing, refunding, or troubleshooting tickets on the website/app, including season tickets and advance releases.
intents.hard_case: “Can I reserve a seat on the 09:15 to Bristol?” – This is a seat reservation request, not a purchase issue, so it belongs to seat_reservation.
intents.disposition_rationale: May require checking account or availability; a human drafts the response.

intents.name: seat_reservation
intents.definition: Customer asks to reserve, confirm, change or query a seat reservation on a specific service.
intents.hard_case: “Why is my train so crowded today?” – This is a capacity complaint, not a reservation query, so it belongs to capacity_requests.
intents.disposition_rationale: Needs to check reservation system; human assistance required.

intents.name: capacity_and_overcrowding
intents.definition: Customer complains about overcrowding, lack of carriages or seats and requests additional capacity or fewer passengers.
intents.hard_case: “Can you add another carriage to the 06:32 Didcot‑Paddington?” – This is a request for extra carriages (capacity), not a seat reservation.

intents.name: compensation_and_refunds
intents.definition: Customer seeks monetary compensation, refund or claim status for a past delay, cancellation or poor service.
intents.hard_case: “Why was the 17:06 Pad‑Westbury cancelled?” – This asks for the reason, not compensation, so it belongs to live_disruption_status.
intents.disposition_rationale: Compensation requires policy checks and possibly account data.

intents.name: service_information_general
intents.definition: Customer asks for static or schedule‑related information that does not need real‑time data: new train schedules, future service availability, tomorrow’s service, coach count, or general service queries.
intents.hard_case: “How many coaches will the 07:33 Pang‑Paddington have today?” – If the user asks for today’s count, it needs live data and belongs to live_disruption_status; only future‑date queries stay here.
intents.disposition_rationale: Answers can be drawn from published timetables.

intents.name: onboard_service_and_facilities
intents.definition: Customer raises issues or asks questions about onboard amenities, seating comfort, accessibility, Wi‑Fi, toilets, or staff behaviour.
intents.hard_case: “The Wi‑Fi was unusable, and the train kept getting later.” – This mixes a Wi‑Fi complaint with a delay; the primary intent is a live disruption status, so it belongs to live_disruption_status.
intents.disposition_rationale: Often needs a human to acknowledge and possibly forward to operations.

intents.name: positive_feedback
intents.definition: Customer expresses appreciation, compliments or positive experience.
intents.hard_case: “Great journey, but the train was 10 minutes late.” – The presence of a complaint pushes it to live_disruption_status.
intents.disposition_rationale: Can be replied with a thank‑you template.

intents.name: other
intents.definition: Any message that does not fit the above intents, including spam, unrelated chatter, or ambiguous multi‑intent messages that cannot be cleanly classified.
intents.hard_case: “Can I get a replacement taxi pls?” – This is a request for a replacement bus, which belongs to replacement_bus_info; if the bot cannot recognise it, it falls here.
intents.disposition_rationale: Human must decide the appropriate handling.

merges_explained: Clusters were merged based on identical handling pathways. All live‑status queries (delays, cancellations, driver absence, platform) became live_disruption_status. All compensation‑related clusters were grouped under compensation_and_refunds because they all require policy lookup and claim processing. Ticket purchase, website issues and advance‑ticket queries share the same support flow (guide, troubleshoot, link) and form ticket_purchase_and_booking. Capacity‑related complaints (extra carriages, overcrowding, standing‑room) were merged into capacity_and_overcrowding. Static schedule queries (new trains, future coach count, tomorrow’s service) formed service_information_general. Onboard amenity complaints and staff behaviour were combined into onboard_service_and_facilities. Positive feedback stayed separate. The catch‑all other captures multi‑intent or noisy messages.
dropped: No clusters were dropped as noise; all were assigned to an intent or the catch‑all.
